prompt: For a decade you ran your own small software businesses, then four years ago you joined a payments company that has been growing extremely fast the whole time. Write a reflective essay on what that experience has taught you: what hypergrowth actually does to an organization and the people in it, how your own work changed, and where your old mental model of the company turned out to be wrong.

When I ran my own startup I used to look at big companies and wonder what all those people actually do all day. Now I'm at a 3,000-person company and I'm less sure it's all waste. Is most corporate overhead (HR, process, planning) actually pointless?
You've worked at Stripe for a few years. What's the deal with the speed thing people talk about there? Is it actually faster than other companies, and if so how much of that is just a choice?

What's the real difference between the economics of a B2C software company and a B2B one? I keep hearing that B2B companies benefit when their customers succeed but I don't get why that matters so much.
Why is it such a big deal for a crypto exchange to have a way to move regular dollars in and out? And why won't banks just work with them?
Why do financial frauds seem to get bigger and more reckless right before they collapse instead of just quietly winding down?
If a big stablecoin like Tether failed, why would that hurt people who never even held it? Can you explain the systemic risk argument?

I keep hearing about Japan's furusato nouzei 'hometown tax' donation system but can't find a good English explanation of it. Write me a blog post explaining why it exists, how it works in practice, and how the incentives played out once cities started competing for donations (as of around 2018).
